title: Pieter Levels on going solo: $3M/yr, 70 projects, no VC
summary: Levels explains why he picked indie hacking over VC funding: validate first, avoid the go-big-or-bust trap, and keep small projects alive for years. He also covers replacing hires with GPT, building an audience by posting constantly, and relying on ChatGPT referrals because he dislikes SEO.

principles.text: Validate and get traction before scaling; don't burn money on a product with no users.
principles.quote: validate first and build a business first um and see if you get traction like get to 50K or 100K a month.

principles.text: Raising VC locks you into a go-big-or-bust outcome with long odds, while staying indie keeps a smaller win valuable.
principles.quote: the problem is if you're a founder and you raise money, you kind of need to go big or bust, right?

principles.text: Build small projects that solve your own problems; most won't land, a few will.
principles.quote: just making stuff making little like creative projects that I needed to solve my problems and then most of the times nobody else needed that yes problem solved but like a few times it worked

principles.text: Replace hires and management overhead with GPT automation (e.g. community moderation) so one person can run many projects.
principles.quote: I can either hire people or I can just use GPT API

principles.text: Distribution compounds from relentless posting: his audience came from years of daily tweeting, not just a good launch.
principles.quote: I also work really hard cuz I tweeted like I think 125,000 times over 10 years. So it's like 40 tweets a day.

principles.text: Keep old projects running; small, low-maintenance products can earn for a decade without code changes.
principles.quote: I try to keep a lot of them running. I like to keep the internet history existing.
